# AF 第二章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 2

[P01] Three nights later old Major died peacefully（平静地） in his sleep. His body was buried at the foot of the Orchard（果园） in early March. This was early in March. During the next three months there was much secret activity. Major's speech had given the more clever animals a completely new outlook（看法） on life. They did not know when the uprising（起义） predicted by Major would take place, they had no reason for thinking that it would be within their own lifetime, but they saw clearly that it was their duty to prepare for it. The work of teaching and organising the others fell naturally upon the pigs, who were generally recognised as being the cleverest of the animals.

[P02] The most important among the pigs were two young boars（公猪） named Snowball and Napoleon, whom Mr. Jones was raising for sale. Napoleon was a large, fierce-looking Berkshire（伯克郡） boar（公猪）, the only one on the farm, not much of a talker, but with a name for getting his own way. Snowball was more lively than Napoleon, quicker in speech and more clever at new ideas, but not thought to have the same depth of character. The other male（雄性） pigs were fat pigs. The best known was a small fat pig named Squealer, with round cheeks, bright eyes, quick movements, and a high, sharp（锋利） voice. He was a brilliant（聪明的） talker, and when arguing some difficult point he jumped from side to side and waved his tail, which was very persuasive（有说服力）.

[P03] The others said of Squealer that he could turn black into white. These three had worked old Major's teachings（教导） into a complete system of thought, and to this they gave the name of Animalism（动物主义）. Several nights a week, after Mr. Jones was asleep, they held secret meetings in the barn（谷仓） and explained the principles（原则） of Animalism to the others.

[P04] At first they met with much stupidity（愚蠢） and not caring. Some animals talked of loyalty（忠诚） to Mr. Jones, whom they called "Master," or said, "Mr. Jones feeds us. If he were gone, we should starve（饿死） to death." Others asked, "Why should we care what happens after we are dead?" or "If this uprising is to happen anyway, what difference does it make whether we work for it or not?" But the pigs had a hard time showing this was against the spirit of Animalism. The pigs had great difficulty making them see this was against the spirit of Animalism. The stupidest questions of all were asked by Mollie, the white mare（母马）.

[P05] The very first question she asked Snowball was: "Will there still be sugar after the uprising?" "No," said Snowball firmly. "We have no way of making sugar on this farm. Besides, you do not need sugar. You will have all the oats（燕麦） and hay（干草） you want." "And shall I still be allowed to wear ribbons（丝带） in my mane（鬃毛）?" "Comrade," asked Mollie."Comrade（同志）," said Snowball, "those ribbons that you are so devoted（忠诚的） to are the badge（标志） of slavery. Can you not understand that liberty（自由） is worth more than ribbons?" Mollie agreed, but she did not sound very convinced（确信）. The pigs had an even harder struggle（斗争） to counteract（抵制） the lies put about by Moses, the tame（驯服） raven（乌鸦）.

[P06] Moses, who was Mr. Jones's special pet, was a spy（间谍） and a tale-teller, but he was also a clever talker. He said he knew of a mysterious country called Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain, to which all animals went when they died. It was somewhere up in the sky, a little way beyond the clouds, Moses said. In Sugarcandy Mountain it was Sunday seven days a week, clover was in season all the year round, and lump（块） sugar and linseed（亚麻籽） cake grew on the hedges（树篱）. The animals hated Moses because he told tales and did no work, but some believed in Sugarcandy Mountain, and the pigs had to argue hard to persuade them that there was no such place. Their most faithful（忠诚） followers（追随者） were Boxer and Clover.

[P07] These two had great difficulty in thinking anything out for themselves, but once they accepted the pigs as their teachers, they took in everything and passed it on to the other animals by simple arguments（争论）. They never missed the secret meetings in the barn, and led the singing of 'animals of England', with which the meetings always ended.

Now, as it turned out, the uprising was achieved much earlier and more easily than Disciple had expected, and they sang 'Animals of England'.In past years Mr. Jones, although a hard master, had been a capable（有能力） farmer, but of late he had fallen on evil days. He had become much disheartened（沮丧） after losing money in a lawsuit（诉讼）, and had taken to drinking more than was good for him.

[P08] For whole days he would lounge（休息室） in his Windsor（温莎） chair in the kitchen, reading newspapers, drinking, and sometimes feeding Moses with crusts of bread soaked（湿透） in beer. His men were idle and dishonest（不诚实）, the fields were full of weeds（杂草）, the buildings needed roofing, the hedges were neglected（被忽视）, and the animals were not fed enough. June came and the hay was almost ready for cutting. On Midsummer's Eve, which was a Saturday, Mr. Jones went into Willingdon and got so drunk at the Red Lion that he did not come back till midday on Sunday.

[P09] The men had milked the cows early and then went out rabbiting, without feeding the animals. When Mr. Jones got back he went straight to sleep on the drawing-room sofa with the News of the World over his face, so when evening came, the animals were still unfed（未喂食）. At last they could stand it no longer. One of the cows broke in the door of the store-shed with her horn and all the animals began to help themselves from the bins. Just then Mr. Jones woke up. The next moment he and his four men were in the store-shed with whips, lashing（鞭打） out in all directions.

[P10] This was too much for the hungry animals to bear. With one accord（一致）, though nothing of the kind had been planned before, they threw themselves upon their tormentors（折磨者）. Jones and his men suddenly found themselves being butted and kicked from all sides. The situation was quite out of their control. They had never seen animals behave like this before, and this sudden uprising of creatures（生物） whom they were used to beating and treating badly just as they chose, frightened them almost out of their wits（智慧）. After only a moment or two they stopped trying to defend（保卫） themselves and ran away as fast as they could. A minute later all five of them were running away down the cart-track that led to the main road, with the animals chasing（追赶） them in triumph（胜利）.

[P11] Jones looked out of the bedroom window, saw what was happening, threw a few things into a bag, and slipped（滑倒） out by another way. Moses sprang（跳起） off his perch and flapped（拍打） after her, croaking（呱呱叫） loudly. Meanwhile（同时） the animals had chased（追赶） Jones and his men out on to the road and slammed（猛关） the five-barred（阻挡） gate behind them. And so, almost before they knew what was happening, the uprising had been carried through: Jones was expelled（驱逐）, and the farm was theirs. For the first few minutes the animals could hardly believe in their good fortune（运气）. Their first act was to gallop（疾驰） in a body right round the boundaries（边界） of the farm, as though to make sure that no human being was hiding anywhere upon it; then they raced back to the farm buildings to wipe（擦） out the last traces（痕迹） of Jones's hated reign（统治）.

[P12] The harness（马具）-room at the end of the stables was broken open; the bits, the nose-rings, the dog-chains, the cruel knives with which Mr. Jones had been used to cut the pigs and lambs, were all thrown down the well. The reins（缰绳）, the halters（笼头）, the blinkers（眼罩）, the degrading（丢脸） nosebags（饲料袋）, were thrown on to the rubbish fire which was burning in the yard. So were the whips. All the animals jumped about with joy when they saw the whips going up in flames. Snowball also threw on to the fire the ribbons with which the horses' manes and tails had usually been decorated on market days, ribbons, Gallop, Boundary（边界）, Reign, Bit, Nose, Chain, Castrate（阉割）, Rein, Halter, Blinker（眼罩）, Degrading, Nosebag and Caper."Ribbons," he said, "should be considered as clothes, which are the mark of a human being.

[P13] All animals should go naked（裸体）." When Boxer heard this, he brought the small straw hat he wore in summer to keep flies out of his ears, and threw it on to the fire with the rest, and in a very little while the animals had destroyed everything that reminded them of Mr. Jones. In a very little while, the animals had destroyed everything that reminded them of Mr. Jones. Napoleon then led them back to the store-shed and gave out a double ration（配给） of corn to everybody, with two biscuits for each dog. Then they sang 'Beasts（野兽） of England' seven times running, and after that they settled down for the night and slept as they had never slept before. But they woke at dawn（黎明） as usual, and suddenly remembering the glorious（光荣） thing that had happened, they all raced out into the pasture（牧场） together.

[P14] A little way down the pasture there was a knoll（小丘） that gave a view of most of the farm. The animals rushed to the top and looked round in the clear morning light. Yes, it was theirs—everything they could see was theirs! In the joy of that thought they jumped round and round, they threw themselves into the air in great leaps（跳跃） of excitement. They rolled in the dew（露水）, they ate mouthfuls（满口） of the sweet summer grass, they kicked up clods（土块） of the black earth and breathed its rich scent（气味）. Then they made a tour of the whole farm and looked with wonder at the ploughland（耕地）, the hayfield（干草地）, the orchard, the pool, the spinney（小树林）.

[P15] It was as though they had never seen these things before, and even now they could hardly believe that it was all their own. Then they filed back to the farm buildings and stopped in silence outside the door of the farmhouse（农舍）. That was theirs too, but they were frightened to go inside. After a moment, however, Snowball and Napoleon butted the door open with their shoulders and the animals went in one by one, walking with the greatest care for fear of troubling anything. They went on tiptoe（踮脚） from room to room, afraid to speak above a whisper（低语） and looking with a kind of awe（敬畏） at the unbelievable（难以置信） wealth, at the beds with their feather（羽毛） mattresses（床垫）, the looking-glasses, the horsehair（马毛） sofa, the Brussels（布鲁塞尔） carpet（地毯）, the lithograph（石版画） of Queen Victoria（维多利亚） over the drawing-room mantelpiece（壁炉架）.

[P16] They were just coming down the stairs when they found Mollie was missing. Going back, the others found she had stayed behind in the best bedroom. She had taken a blue ribbon（丝带） from Mrs. Jones's dressing-table, and was holding it against her shoulder and admiring herself in the glass in a very foolish way. The others scolded（责骂） her sharply（尖锐地）, and they went outside. Some hams hanging in the kitchen were taken out for burial（埋葬）, and the barrel（桶） of beer in the scullery（洗碗间） was broken open with a kick from Boxer's hoof（蹄）. Otherwise（否则） nothing in the house was touched. They all agreed that the farmhouse should be kept as a museum.

[P17] All agreed that no animal must ever live there. They decided this on the spot（地点）, all of them together. The animals had their breakfast, and then Snowball and Napoleon called them together again. "Comrades（同志们）," said Snowball, "it is half-past six and we have a long day before us. Today we begin the hay harvest. But there is another matter that must be attended to first." The pigs now revealed（揭示） that during the past three months they had taught themselves to read and write from an old spelling book. It had belonged to Mr. Jones's children and had been thrown on the rubbish heap（堆）.

[P18] Napoleon sent for pots of black and white paint and led the way down to the five-barred（阻挡） gate that opened onto the main road. Then Snowball (for it was Snowball who was best at writing) took a brush between the two knuckles（指关节） of his trotter（猪蹄）, painted out FARM from the top bar（酒吧） and in its place painted ANIMAL FARM. This was to be the name of the farm from now on. After this they went back to the farm buildings, where Snowball and Napoleon sent for a ladder and had it set against the end wall of the big barn. They explained that by their studies of the past three months the pigs had succeeded in reducing the principles of Animalism to Seven Commandments（戒律）.

[P19] These Seven Commandments would now be written on the wall; they would make a law that could not be changed, and all the animals on Animal Farm must live by it for ever after. It was not easy, but Snowball climbed up with some difficulty and began to work, with Squealer a few rungs below him holding the paint-pot. The Commandments were written on the tarred（涂焦油） wall in great white letters that could be read thirty yards away. They were these: THE SEVEN COMMANDMENTS 1. Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy. Whatever goes upon four legs, or has wings, is a friend.

[P20] No animal shall wear clothes. No animal shall sleep in a bed. No animal shall drink alcohol（酒精）. No animal shall kill any other animal. All animals are equal. It was very neatly（整洁地） written, and except that "friend" was written "freind（朋友）" and one of the "S's" was the wrong way round, the spelling was correct all the way through. Snowball read it aloud for the others. All the animals nodded in agreement, and the cleverer ones began to learn the Commandments by heart. "Now, comrades," cried Snowball, throwing down the paint-brush, "to the hayfield! Let us make it a point of honour to get in the harvest more quickly than Jones and his men could do. But at this moment the 3 cows, who had seemed uneasy for some time past, set up a loud lowing. But then the three cows, who had seemed uneasy（不安） for some time past, set up a loud lowing.

[P21] They had not been milked for twenty-four hours, and their udders（乳房） were almost bursting（爆裂）. After a little thought, the pigs sent for buckets and milked the cows quite well, their trotters（猪蹄） being just right for this task. Soon there were five buckets of frothing creamy（奶油色） milk, and many of the animals looked at them with great interest. "What is going to happen to all that milk?" said someone. "Jones used sometimes to mix some of it in our mash（糊状饲料）," said one of the hens. "Never mind the milk, comrades!" cried Napoleon, placing himself in front of the buckets. "That will be attended to. The harvest is more important. Comrade Snowball will lead the way.

[P22] I shall follow in a few minutes. Forward, comrades! The hay is waiting." So the animals trooped（成群） down to the hayfield to begin the harvest, and when they came back in the evening, the milk had disappeared. Mash Troop（一群）
